Leonidas I. A Spartan king who reigned during four hundred eighty BCE, remembered as the legendary commander who led Greece's most famous act of defiant resistance against Xerxes' invading Persian Empire. At the narrow pass of Thermopylae in four hundred eighty BCE, Leonidas commanded roughly seven thousand Greek hoplites, including three hundred elite Spartan warriors, against an overwhelmingly larger Persian force.

One of two Spartan kings, Sparta maintained a dual kingship, and Leonidas reigned during the Persian Wars, the defining conflict of classical Greece in the fifth century BCE. He chose to hold the pass at Thermopylae with a small contingent when Xerxes invaded Greece, blocking the only major route into central Greece through narrow mountain terrain.

His three hundred Spartan elite were reinforced by hoplites from other Greek city-states. Together they held the narrow pass for two days against vastly larger Persian forces estimated at one hundred thousand or more. He died at Thermopylae when a traitor revealed a mountain path allowing Persians to outflank his position. He famously ordered the remaining Greeks to retreat while he held the pass to the death.

The stand at Thermopylae gave other Greek forces critical time to organize their overall resistance and ultimately contributed to the Persian defeat at Plataea later that year. His legend epitomized Spartan values of honor, self-sacrifice, and unwavering commitment to duty, making him an immortal hero figure across Greek culture and Western tradition. He connects to Sparta his kingdom, to the Battle of Thermopylae where he died and achieved immortality, and to Xerxes the Persian emperor against whom he made his stand.
